civs.romans: Rome began as a cluster of farming villages on the Tiber and grew, through centuries of war, law and road-building, into an empire that ringed the Mediterranean. Julius Caesar, soldier, author and finally dictator, conquered Gaul and steered the old Republic toward one-man rule. Militaristic and commercial, Rome promotes its winners twice as often and draws extra commerce from rich tiles. Its Legionary hits as hard as a Swordsman but defends at 3, so the same unit can take a city and then hold it.
civs.egyptians: Egypt grew along the Nile, whose yearly flood fed a kingdom of pharaohs, priests and pyramid builders for three thousand years. Cleopatra, the last queen of its Ptolemaic line, bargained with Rome's mightiest men to keep her country free. Religious and industrious, Egypt shrugs off anarchy in one turn, builds Temples and Cathedrals at half price and improves land 50% faster. The War Chariot, a chariot with double the attack, invites an early raid, and the Pyramids alone can start Egypt's golden age.
civs.greeks: The Greeks lived in rival city-states scattered over rocky peninsulas and islands, yet together they gave the world philosophy, theatre, geometry and the idea of citizens governing themselves. Alexander of Macedon united them by force and marched as far as India before he was thirty-three. Commercial and scientific, Greece enjoys low corruption, rich tiles, half-price Libraries and Marketplaces and a free advance with every new era. The Hoplite, a spearman that defends at 3, guards that growing wealth cheaply.
civs.babylonians: Babylon stood on the Euphrates as the great city of Mesopotamia, famed for its astronomers, its gardens and its mighty walls. Hammurabi, its best-remembered king, had his laws carved in stone so that every subject could know them. Scientific and religious, Babylon builds Libraries and Temples at half cost, gains a free advance with each new era and passes through revolutions in a single turn. Its Bowman, an archer that defends at 2, protects the early cities while culture piles up.
civs.germans: For centuries the German lands were a patchwork of small kingdoms, duchies and free cities. Otto von Bismarck, Prussia's iron-willed chancellor, forged them into a single empire in 1871 through shrewd diplomacy and three short wars. Militaristic and scientific, Germany promotes its winners twice as often, builds Barracks and Libraries at half cost and gains a free advance with each new era. The Panzer, a tank with three moves instead of two, is a late but devastating tool for breaking enemy lines.
civs.russians: From the river towns of Kiev and Novgorod, Russia spread across forest and steppe until it spanned two continents. Catherine the Great, a German princess who took the throne in a palace coup, pushed its borders south and west and welcomed Enlightenment thinkers to her court. Expansionist and scientific, Russia starts with a Scout to find good land, builds Libraries cheaply and gains a free advance with each era. The Cossack, a cavalry unit with blitz, can strike several times in one turn.
civs.chinese: China is one of the oldest continuous civilizations, a land of rice terraces, imperial examinations, paper, printing and gunpowder. Mao Zedong led the Communist revolution to victory in 1949 and ruled the People's Republic for almost three decades. Militaristic and industrious, China promotes veterans twice as fast, builds Barracks and Walls cheaply, improves land 50% faster and adds a shield to every city of size 7 or more. The Rider, a knight with three moves, makes a fast medieval strike force.
civs.americans: The United States grew from thirteen Atlantic colonies into a continental nation of immigrants, farms and factories. Abraham Lincoln, a self-taught lawyer from the frontier, held the Union together through a bitter civil war and ended slavery. Expansionist and industrious, America starts with a Scout, improves land 50% faster and gains an extra shield in cities of size 7 and more. The F-15, a jet fighter whose bombing can destroy units outright, gives America command of the late-game skies.
civs.japanese: Japan's island realm took ideas from the mainland, from writing to Buddhism, and made them its own under emperors and, in practice, warrior lords. Tokugawa Ieyasu won the long struggle of the warring states and founded a shogunate that kept the peace for more than 250 years. Militaristic and religious, Japan promotes its winners twice as often, builds Barracks and Temples at half cost and survives revolutions in one turn. The Samurai, a knight that defends at 4, holds ground as well as it attacks.
civs.french: France grew out of the western Frankish kingdom into one of Europe's great powers, a centre of cathedrals, philosophy, revolution and fine food. Joan of Arc, a peasant girl guided by the voices of saints, led French troops to lift the siege of Orleans and was burned at the stake at nineteen. Commercial and industrious, France enjoys low corruption, extra commerce, cheap Marketplaces and fast workers. The Musketeer, a musketman that defends at 5, makes French cities very hard to crack.
civs.indians: India's civilization reaches back to the cities of the Indus valley and gave the world great religions, epic poetry and the decimal numbers we count with. Mohandas Gandhi led its struggle for independence from Britain through non-violent resistance and became a worldwide symbol of peaceful protest. Commercial and religious, India builds Temples and Marketplaces cheaply, suffers little corruption and only one turn of anarchy. The War Elephant needs neither horses nor iron and carries an extra hit point, so India can field knights without strategic resources.
civs.persians: Persia built the first great empire to stretch from the Aegean to the Indus, linked by royal roads and governed by satraps who mostly respected local custom. Xerxes, son of Darius, led an enormous army into Greece and burned Athens before his fleet was beaten at Salamis. Scientific and industrious, Persia gains a free advance with each era, builds Libraries cheaply and improves land 50% faster. The Immortals, swordsmen with attack 4, give it an early army that can win wars.
civs.aztecs: The Aztecs founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco and made it the heart of a tribute empire of floating gardens and towering temples. Montezuma ruled at its height, only to see the city fall to Spanish invaders and their native allies. Militaristic and agricultural, the Aztecs promote often, gain extra food on every city tile and build Barracks and Aqueducts cheaply. The Jaguar Warrior, cheap and moving two tiles, is ready from the first turn for exploring and early raids.
civs.zulu: The Zulu were a small clan of southern Africa until Shaka transformed them in the early nineteenth century. He drilled his regiments in close-quarter fighting and gathered many neighbouring peoples into a powerful kingdom. Militaristic and expansionist, the Zulu start with a Scout, promote their winners twice as often and build Barracks at half cost. The Impi, a spearman that moves two tiles, lets them cover a wide frontier early and push their settlers outward under guard.
civs.iroquois: The Iroquois Confederacy joined five, and later six, nations of the northeastern woodlands under a Great Law of Peace that balanced the voices of chiefs and clan mothers. Hiawatha, remembered as one of its founders, carried the message of union from village to village. Commercial and agricultural, the Iroquois enjoy low corruption, extra commerce and an extra food on every city tile. The Mounted Warrior, a horseman with attack 3, is an early raider of real power.
civs.english: England, an island kingdom on Europe's western edge, became a naval and trading power whose empire and language spread around the globe. Elizabeth I ruled for forty-five years, saw off the Spanish Armada and presided over a flowering of theatre and exploration. Commercial and seafaring, England enjoys low corruption and rich tiles, builds Harbors and Marketplaces cheaply and sails one tile farther. The Man-O-War, a frigate with stronger guns that can seize beaten ships, rules the seas in the age of sail.
civs.mongols: The Mongols were nomad clans of the eastern steppe, masters of the horse and the bow. Temujin united them and, as Genghis Khan, launched conquests that built the largest land empire in history, from the Pacific to Eastern Europe. Militaristic and expansionist, the Mongols start with a Scout, promote twice as often and build Barracks cheaply. The Keshik, a medieval horseman that crosses hills and mountains as easily as open ground, lets them strike from where nobody expects.
civs.spanish: Spain was forged in the long reconquest of Iberia and, under its Catholic monarchs, opened the Americas to Europe. Isabella of Castile united the country with her husband Ferdinand and backed the voyage of Columbus in 1492. Religious and seafaring, Spain builds Temples and Harbors cheaply, survives anarchy in a single turn and sails one tile farther. The Conquistador treats every tile as a road, making it a superb explorer and a raider of distant lands.
civs.vikings: The Norse of Scandinavia sailed their longships far and wide as raiders, traders and settlers, from the rivers of Russia to Iceland, Greenland and North America. Ragnar Lodbrok, a hero of the sagas, is said to have plundered England and France. Militaristic and seafaring, the Vikings promote twice as often, sail one tile farther and build Harbors and Barracks at half cost. The Berserk, with attack 6, can storm a beach straight from its ship.
civs.ottomans: The Ottomans began as a small Turkish principality in Anatolia and grew into an empire spanning three continents, ruled from Constantinople after 1453. Osman I, its founder, gave the dynasty its name and its first conquests. Scientific and industrious, the Ottomans gain a free advance with each era, build Libraries cheaply and improve land 50% faster. The Sipahi, a cavalry unit with attack 8, is the strongest mounted force of its age.
civs.celts: The Celts spread over much of ancient Europe, a people of hill forts, druids, bards and splendid metalwork. Brennus led a Gallic army that sacked Rome around 390 BC, a humiliation the Romans never forgot. Religious and agricultural, the Celts build Temples and Aqueducts cheaply, pass through anarchy in a single turn and gain extra food on every city tile. The Gallic Swordsman, a swordsman that moves two tiles, makes them dangerous neighbours early on.
civs.arabs: Within a century of leaving the Arabian peninsula, the early Muslim community reached from Spain to Central Asia, carrying a new faith, a language of learning and wide trade networks. Abu Bakr, the first caliph, held that young community together after the death of Muhammad. Expansionist and religious, Arabia starts with a Scout, builds Temples cheaply and survives revolutions in one turn. The Ansar Warrior, a knight that moves three tiles, covers long distances quickly.
civs.carthaginians: Carthage was a Phoenician colony in North Africa that grew into a trading empire across the western Mediterranean. Hannibal marched elephants over the Alps and defeated Roman armies in Italy for fifteen years, yet Carthage itself was destroyed in the end. Industrious and seafaring, Carthage improves land 50% faster, sails one tile farther and builds Harbors cheaply. The Numidian Mercenary, a spearman that defends at 3 and attacks at 2, is a versatile early guard.
civs.koreans: Korea developed a distinctive culture on its mountainous peninsula, printing with movable metal type and creating its own phonetic alphabet. Wang Kon founded the Goryeo dynasty in 918 and reunified the peninsula, giving Korea the name the world still uses. Commercial and scientific, Korea enjoys low corruption, extra commerce, cheap Libraries and Marketplaces and a free advance with each era. The Hwach'a, a cannon whose bombardment can destroy units outright, makes Korean sieges deadly.
civs.sumerians: Sumer, in southern Mesopotamia, built some of the first cities, irrigation canals, written records and law codes in history. Gilgamesh, a king of Uruk, became the hero of the oldest surviving epic, in which he searches for immortality after losing his friend Enkidu. Scientific and agricultural, Sumeria gains extra food on every city tile, builds Libraries cheaply and gains a free advance with each era. The Enkidu Warrior, a warrior that defends at 2, guards the first cities without any advance.
civs.hittites: The Hittites ruled much of Anatolia in the second millennium BC from their capital Hattusa, contesting Syria with Egypt. Mursilis I carried their power far enough to sack Babylon around 1595 BC. Commercial and expansionist, the Hittites start with a Scout, enjoy low corruption and extra commerce and build Marketplaces cheaply. The Three-Man Chariot, a chariot with attack and defence 2, is one of the strongest units of the early game.
civs.dutch: The Dutch won their land from the sea with dikes and windmills, then won their independence from Spain and built a trading empire reaching the East Indies. William of Orange led the revolt that founded the Dutch Republic. Agricultural and seafaring, the Netherlands gain extra food on every city tile, sail one tile farther and build Harbors and Aqueducts cheaply. The Swiss Mercenary, a pikeman that defends at 4, holds cities steadily through the Middle Ages.
civs.portuguese: Portugal, a small kingdom on the Atlantic edge of Iberia, led Europe into the age of exploration, rounding Africa and reaching India, Brazil and Japan. Prince Henry, remembered as the Navigator, sponsored the sailors and map-makers who started it all. Expansionist and seafaring, Portugal starts with a Scout, sails one tile farther and builds Harbors cheaply. The Carrack, a sturdier caravel that can cross open ocean, carries its settlers and explorers to distant shores.
civs.byzantines: The Byzantine Empire was the eastern half of Rome, which outlived the west by a thousand years, ruling from Constantinople and preserving Greek learning. Empress Theodora, once an actress, became Justinian's partner in power and stood firm when riots nearly toppled the throne. Scientific and seafaring, Byzantium gains a free advance with each era, builds Libraries and Harbors cheaply and sails one tile farther. The Dromon, an early warship whose bombardment can sink ships, rules the coastal seas.
civs.inca: The Inca built the largest empire of the pre-Columbian Americas along the spine of the Andes, joined by mountain roads, rope bridges and relay runners. Pachacuti turned the small kingdom of Cusco into that empire in the fifteenth century. Expansionist and agricultural, the Inca start with their own Chasqui Scout instead of a Scout and gain extra food on every city tile, which makes for fast early growth. Their Chasqui Scout crosses hills and mountains as easily as flat land and can defend itself while it explores.
civs.maya: The Maya raised cities of stone pyramids and palaces in the rainforests of Central America, with a writing system and a calendar of remarkable precision. Smoke-Jaguar ruled the city of Copan in the seventh century, an age of ambitious building. Industrious and agricultural, the Maya improve land 50% faster, gain extra food on every city tile and build Aqueducts cheaply. The Javelin Thrower, an archer that defends at 2, can turn defeated enemies into captive workers.

traits.militaristic: Victorious units are promoted twice as often, 1 win in 4 instead of 1 in 8. Military improvements such as Barracks, City Walls, Coastal Fortresses, Harbors and Airports cost half.
traits.religious: A revolution brings only a single turn of anarchy. Temples and Cathedrals cost half.
traits.commercial: Every tile that already makes at least 2 commerce makes 1 more, and the empire counts 25% more optimal cities, which lowers corruption. Marketplaces, Banks, Stock Exchanges, Harbors and other trade buildings cost half.
traits.industrious: Workers finish their jobs 50% faster, and every city of size 7 or more makes an extra shield on its city tile.
traits.expansionist: The civilization starts the game with a Scout (or its own unique version, such as the Inca Chasqui Scout), and only expansionist civilizations can build Scouts, ideal for early exploring and tribal villages.
traits.scientific: A free advance arrives each time the civilization enters a new era, and being first in the world to an advance has a 10% chance to bring a scientific great leader. Libraries, Universities and Research Labs cost half.
traits.agricultural: Every land city makes 1 extra food on its city tile. Aqueducts, Recycling Centers and Solar Plants cost half.
traits.seafaring: Ships move one tile farther each turn. Harbors, Offshore Platforms, Commercial Docks and Coastal Fortresses cost half.

cities.title: Cities
cities.summary: Cities are where your people live, eat, work the land and build everything your civilization needs.
cities.body:
A [Settler](pedia:units/settler) founds a city on the tile it stands on, as long as it has movement left. Cities cannot be placed on water, mountains or volcanoes, inside another civilization's borders, or right next to another city: at least one tile must lie between them. A new city starts at size 1 with a road on its tile and a small border, and your first city receives the [Palace](pedia:buildings/palace). Settlers and Workers can also join an existing city to add to its population.

Every citizen eats 2 food. The food left over fills the food box, which holds 10 × (size + 1): 20 food to grow from size 1, 70 from size 6. When the box is full the city grows by one and the box empties; a [Granary](pedia:buildings/granary) keeps half of it. A food deficit drains the box, and a city that runs dry shrinks by one (a size-1 city never starves away completely).

Cities come in three sizes:
- Town: size 1 to 6. Growing past 6 needs an [Aqueduct](pedia:buildings/aqueduct), unless the town sits on a river or beside a fresh-water lake.
- City: size 7 to 12. Growing past 12 needs a [Hospital](pedia:buildings/hospital).
- Metropolis: size 13 and up.

Size matters beyond population. Bigger cities give their defenders a larger bonus, and under most governments they support more units for free. A city that has reached its limit keeps its food box full until it gets the building it needs.

tiles.title: Tiles and Yields
tiles.summary: Every city draws food, shields and commerce from the tiles its citizens work.

production.title: Production
production.summary: Shields build every unit, improvement and wonder, and can be hurried with gold or forced labour.
production.body:
A city's shields come from its worked tiles. Waste takes its share first ([corruption](pedia:concepts/corruption)), then buildings multiply what remains: [Factory](pedia:buildings/factory) +50%, [Manufacturing Plant](pedia:buildings/manufacturingPlant) +50%, a power plant raising the factory bonus further, [Iron Works](pedia:buildings/ironWorks) +100%. Civil Engineers add 2 shields each toward buildings and wonders. A city in disorder produces nothing.

When the shield box reaches the item's cost, it completes at the end of the turn; shields beyond its cost are lost. Units that cost population, such as Settlers (2) and Workers (1), wait until the city is larger than that cost. A city keeps repeating a unit until you queue something else.

Switching what a city builds, between units, improvements and wonders alike, keeps every shield in the box.

Hurrying finishes the current item at the end of the turn:
- Monarchy, Republic and Democracy pay gold: 4 per missing shield for units, 2 for buildings, double when the box is empty.
- Despotism, Feudalism, Communism and Fascism use forced labour: one citizen per 20 missing shields, and each sacrificed citizen leaves someone unhappy for 20 turns. The city must keep at least one citizen.
- Drafting: once [Nationalism](pedia:techs/nationalism) is known, a city larger than 1 can turn a citizen into the best draftable defender it can build, such as a Rifleman, which comes out as a Conscript. Each city may draft up to its government's limit each turn (2, or 1 under Republic and Democracy), and the citizen left behind is unhappy for 20 turns.
- Anarchy cannot hurry or draft, and nobody can hurry wonders, Wealth or a city in disorder.

[Wealth](pedia:buildings/wealth) turns shields into gold, one per 4 shields, or per 2 after [Economics](pedia:techs/economics). Disbanding a unit inside one of your cities adds half its shield cost to the current build (not to Wealth); disbanded anywhere else it returns nothing. Units upgrade in your cities for 3 gold per shield of difference. Every building costs its upkeep in gold each turn.

trade.title: Trade and the Trade Network
trade.summary: Commerce funds your treasury and research, and roads and harbours tie your cities and resources into one network.
trade.body:
Commerce is the third yield of a tile. It comes mostly from rivers, roads, coasts and some resources. After corruption, each city splits its commerce into tax, science and luxury by your rates ([science](pedia:concepts/science)).

Your cities also form a trade network. Two cities are connected when:
- an unbroken chain of roads or railroads joins them without crossing another civilization's territory (city tiles count as road);
- both have a [Harbor](pedia:buildings/harbor) and water joins them: coast from the start, sea once you know [Astronomy](pedia:techs/astronomy), ocean once you know [Navigation](pedia:techs/navigation).

A city cut off from the capital counts as far away for corruption, so connecting cities pays off immediately.

Luxury and strategic resources serve the whole network. A resource counts once it lies inside your borders, you can see it (strategic resources need their revealing advance) and it is on a road or railroad (a river is not enough), or inside one of your cities' work areas. Every connected city then enjoys the luxury's happiness or may build the units and buildings that need the strategic resource.

Resources can also be traded with other civilizations, but only along a trade route between the two capitals: roads and railroads (not rivers) through either side's land or unclaimed land, or water between harbour cities. If that route breaks, the delivery stops while the deal runs on, and the turn digest tells you.

science.title: Science and Rates
science.summary: Your tax, science and luxury rates divide each city's commerce, and science buys new advances.
science.body:
Each turn, after corruption, a city's commerce is split by your three rates, set in steps of 10%: luxury and science are rounded down and tax takes the rest. Specialists add their own output: a Scientist 3 beakers, a Tax Collector 2 gold, an Entertainer 1 luxury. Buildings then multiply each share: a [Library](pedia:buildings/library), [University](pedia:buildings/university) and [Research Lab](pedia:buildings/researchLab) add 50% science each, and a [Marketplace](pedia:buildings/marketplace), [Bank](pedia:buildings/bank) and [Stock Exchange](pedia:buildings/stockExchange) add 50% tax each.

No rate may exceed the government's cap, which is 100% for every government in these rules. During Anarchy all commerce goes to luxury and research stops.

An advance costs its base cost × 10 × the world size's tech rate ÷ 100 beakers. The tech rate runs from 160 on a Tiny map to 400 on a Huge one, so Bronze Working costs 48 beakers on a Tiny map. Computer players pay their difficulty's factor instead of 10. Advances already known by civilizations you have met are cheaper, by up to 30% when all of them know it.

Research takes at least 4 turns per advance, and beakers beyond the cost are lost when it arrives. After 50 turns on one advance it arrives anyway. Beakers gathered with no target are kept for the next one.

The tree is split into four eras. You enter the next era once you know every required advance of the current one; advances of later eras stay closed until then. Tax pays building upkeep and unit support, and if the treasury would go negative, a building is sold.

corruption.title: Corruption and Waste
corruption.summary: Distance from your capital and the size of your empire cost every city part of its commerce and shields.
corruption.body:
Corruption takes commerce and waste takes shields, at the same rate in each city, before anything else is done with them. The city with your [Palace](pedia:buildings/palace) suffers neither.

A city's rate has two parts:
- Distance: up to 50%, growing with the distance to the nearest seat of government and full at a quarter of the map's width plus height (50 tiles on a Standard map).
- Rank: up to 50%, growing as the city's rank (cities ordered by distance) approaches the optimal city number, and growing further beyond it. The optimal number is the world size's value × the difficulty's percentage: 18 on a Standard map at Regent.

The government scales these: Despotism 90%, Monarchy and Feudalism 75%, Republic and Fascism 60%, and Democracy 40% of the rank part only, so distance does not matter. Communism sets a flat 30% everywhere but the capital, and Anarchy a flat 90%.

Reductions follow: a [Courthouse](pedia:buildings/courthouse) cuts the rate by half, a [Police Station](pedia:buildings/policeStation) by a quarter, and each Policeman specialist by a tenth. A [Forbidden Palace](pedia:buildings/forbiddenPalace), or the [Secret Police HQ](pedia:buildings/secretPoliceHq) under Communism, acts as a second seat of government. Commercial civilizations count 25% more optimal cities, and a celebrating city halves its waste.

Example on a Tiny map under Despotism: a city 6 tiles from the capital with rank 1 loses 12%, connected to it or not, or 6% with a Courthouse.

happiness.title: Happiness and Disorder
happiness.summary: Citizens are happy, content or unhappy, and the balance decides whether a city works, riots or celebrates.

governments.title: Governments
governments.summary: Your government sets corruption, hurrying, worker speed, unit support, drafting, military police and war weariness.
governments.body:
Everyone starts in Despotism; every other government needs its advance.
- [Despotism](pedia:governments/despotism): rampant corruption, −1 on tile yields above 2, forced labour, 4 free units per city, 2 police.
- [Monarchy](pedia:governments/monarchy): problematic corruption, gold hurrying, 2/4/8 free units for town/city/metropolis, 3 police.
- [Feudalism](pedia:governments/feudalism): problematic corruption, forced labour, 5/2/1 free units at 3 gold for each extra, 3 police, low war weariness.
- [Communism](pedia:governments/communism): a flat 30% corruption, forced labour, 6 free units per city, 4 police.
- [Fascism](pedia:governments/fascism): nuisance corruption, forced labour, workers at ×4 speed, 4/7/10 free units, 4 police.
- [Republic](pedia:governments/republic): nuisance corruption, +1 commerce on tiles with commerce, gold hurrying, 1/3/4 free units at 2 gold for each extra, low war weariness.
- [Democracy](pedia:governments/democracy): minimal corruption that ignores distance, +1 commerce, gold hurrying, workers at ×3 speed, no free units, high war weariness.

Once [Nationalism](pedia:techs/nationalism) is known, every government except Anarchy can draft: a city larger than 1 turns a citizen into a Conscript defender, up to 2 units per city each turn (1 under Republic and Democracy), and the citizen left behind is unhappy for 20 turns ([production](pedia:concepts/production)).

Workers work at ×2 under the other governments and ×1 in Anarchy. Units beyond the free number cost 1 gold each per turn unless noted; workers, settlers and explorers are always free.

Changing government starts a revolution: 2 to 5 turns of [Anarchy](pedia:governments/anarchy), chosen at random but never more than the difficulty allows (4 at Monarch down to 1 at Sid). Religious civilizations need only one turn. During Anarchy corruption is a flat 90%, tile yields above 2 lose a point, research stops, all commerce goes to luxury, nothing can be hurried and buildings cost no upkeep. The new government takes over at the start of the turn the anarchy ends.

culture.title: Culture and Borders
culture.summary: Buildings and wonders earn culture, which pushes your borders outward and shapes how other peoples see you.
culture.body:
Every turn each city earns the culture of its buildings: the Palace 1, a Temple 2, a Library 3, a Cathedral 3, and wonders 2 to 8. A building's culture doubles once it has stood for 1000 years on the game calendar; early in the game, at 50 years a turn, that is only 20 turns. Your civilization's culture is the sum of everything its cities have ever produced.

Culture pushes borders outward. A new city claims the ring of tiles around it, and its border grows by one ring when the city's culture reaches 10, 100, 1000, 10000, 20000, 40000 and 80000 points. The second ring covers exactly the city's 21-tile work area, and later rings grow roughly as circles. Where rings overlap, a tile goes to the city with the most influence on it: its culture points divided by its distance to the tile (at least 1). A tie goes to the older city, and a city's own tile is always its owner's.

Borders matter: a city can only work tiles inside them, resources count only inside them, and foreign military units standing in someone else's land annoy the owner unless the two share a right of passage. You always see your own territory.

Comparing two civilizations' culture decides how each people sees the other, from in awe of (three times the culture or more) through admirers, impressed, unimpressed and dismissive to disdainful of (a third or less). That opinion drives resistance in conquered cities, [culture flips](pedia:concepts/cultureFlips) and the success of propaganda ([espionage](pedia:concepts/espionage)).

Culture can also win the game: 100000 points and twice any rival's, or 20000 in a single city ([victory](pedia:concepts/victory)).

cultureFlips.title: Resistance and Culture Flips
cultureFlips.summary: Conquered people may resist, and a city overshadowed by a foreign culture may change sides.

movement.title: Movement
movement.summary: Terrain, roads, railroads and rivers decide how far units travel each turn.
movement.body:
Movement points are counted in thirds so that roads can be cheap.

Entering a tile costs:
- a railroad on both tiles: nothing;
- a road on both tiles: one third of a point;
- otherwise the terrain's cost: 1 for flat land, 2 for hills, forest and marsh, 3 for mountains, jungle and volcanoes;
- ships: 1 per tile.

Some units are special. The [Explorer](pedia:units/explorer) and [Conquistador](pedia:units/conquistador) treat every tile as road, and the [Keshik](pedia:units/keshik) crosses hills and mountains for a single point.

A road does not help across a river until you know [Engineering](pedia:techs/engineering), which bridges rivers. Otherwise crossing a river costs nothing extra.

A unit with any movement left may always make one more step, even into terrain that costs more than it has; the step uses up the rest.

Wheeled units need a road to enter jungle, marsh, mountains or volcanoes. Galleys keep to the coast and some ships cannot enter ocean. While at peace you cannot enter a tile held by another civilization's units; at war, moving there is an attack.

Zones of control: units with that ability (Cavalry, Tanks, Keshiks and others) and armed units inside a fortress watch the eight tiles around them. An enemy land unit moving from one watched tile to another draws a free shot that can cost it a hit point, never its last. Zones of control never block movement.

Goto finds the cheapest known route and keeps walking each turn until the unit arrives.

workers.title: Workers
workers.summary: Workers build roads, irrigation, mines and railroads, alone or as one automated pool.
workers.body:
[Workers](pedia:units/worker) improve the land. A job needs base turns × the terrain's movement cost × 100 points of work, and each worker adds 100 × the government's worker rate per turn: ×1 in Anarchy, ×2 under most governments, ×3 in Democracy and ×4 in Fascism, doubled again with [Replaceable Parts](pedia:techs/replaceableParts). Industrious civilizations work 50% faster. Under Despotism one worker builds a road on grassland in 3 turns and a mine on hills in 12, or 6 with two workers.

Workers on one tile pool their work on the same job, and work is added at the end of the turn.

- [Road](pedia:workerJobs/road): +1 commerce on most land and faster movement.
- [Railroad](pedia:workerJobs/railroad): free movement and +1 shield where the tile yields shields; needs a road, [Steam Power](pedia:techs/steamPower) and Iron.
- [Irrigation](pedia:workerJobs/irrigation): more food; needs fresh water next to the tile until [Electricity](pedia:techs/electricity).
- [Mine](pedia:workerJobs/mine): more shields. Irrigation and a mine replace each other.
- [Fortress](pedia:workerJobs/fortress): a defence bonus, after [Construction](pedia:techs/construction).
- [Clear Forest](pedia:workerJobs/clearForest) sends 10 shields to the nearest city; [Clear Wetlands](pedia:workerJobs/clearWetlands), [Plant Forest](pedia:workerJobs/plantForest) and [Clear Damage](pedia:workerJobs/clearDamage) reshape or clean the land.

Automated workers share one job board. Every city's needs (irrigation for hungry cities, mines for weak producers, roads, railroads, clean-up) plus roads between cities and to resources are scored by your task order, and each idle worker takes the best job less three points per tile of travel. They keep away from visible enemies and never swap a mine for irrigation or back.

combat.title: Combat
combat.summary: Battles are fought in rounds until one side runs out of hit points.

bombard.title: Bombardment
bombard.summary: Artillery, warships and aircraft wear down a tile from a distance without risking themselves.
bombard.body:
Catapults, cannons, artillery, many warships, bombers and cruise missiles can bombard: they fire at an enemy tile without moving onto it. A unit bombards once a turn (blitz units may fire again while they have moves), spends one movement point, and can reach any tile within its bombard range, at least 1 tile away.

Each bombardment fires as many rounds as the unit's rate of fire. A round hits with chance B ÷ (B + D), where B is the bombard strength and D the best defence among the target's units against bombardment, at least 1. [Civil Defense](pedia:buildings/civilDefense) adds 50% to a city's defenders here. Rounds aimed at a city's citizens and buildings face at least the city's own bombard defence: 8 against land bombardment with [City Walls](pedia:buildings/walls) (or the Great Wall), 8 against ships with a [Coastal Fortress](pedia:buildings/coastalFortress). A Catapult then hits a walled city's people only a third of the time. Air strikes ignore both; the [SAM Missile Battery](pedia:buildings/samMissileBattery) covers those. A hit lands, at random, on one of:
- a unit, which loses a hit point;
- a citizen, if the city has more than one;
- an ordinary building, never a wonder or the Palace.

Normal bombardment wounds but never kills: the last hit point always survives. Lethal bombard changes that. Units with lethal land bombard, such as the Korean [Hwach'a](pedia:units/hwacha), the American [F-15](pedia:units/f15) and the [Bomber](pedia:units/bomber), can destroy land units, and lethal sea bombard, such as the Byzantine [Dromon](pedia:units/dromon) and the [Fighter](pedia:units/fighter), can sink ships.

Artillery has no defence of its own and is captured if an enemy reaches it alone, so keep it stacked with defenders. It also fires defensively: when an enemy land unit attacks the stack, each bombard unit that has not fired this turn shoots once at the attacker first.

Cruise missiles are used up when they fire. Aircraft bombard through their missions ([air](pedia:concepts/air)).

experience.title: Experience and Promotion
experience.summary: Units that win battles can rise through four experience levels, gaining hit points and better odds to withdraw.
experience.body:
Every unit has one of four experience levels. The level sets its hit points and its chance to withdraw from a lost battle; it never changes attack or defence, but an extra hit point is often worth more than a strength bonus.
- Conscript: 2 hit points, 34% to withdraw.
- Regular: 3 hit points, 50%.
- Veteran: 4 hit points, 58%.
- Elite: 5 hit points, 66%.

New units are Regular, or Veteran when built in a city with [Barracks](pedia:buildings/barracks) for land units, a [Harbor](pedia:buildings/harbor) for ships or an [Airport](pedia:buildings/airport) for aircraft. The same buildings let units of their kind heal fully in one turn.

A unit that wins a battle may be promoted one level, with a 1 in 8 chance; militaristic civilizations promote twice as often, 1 in 4. Victories over barbarians never lift a unit beyond Veteran, and barbarians themselves are never promoted.

Elite units have one more reward to give. When an Elite unit wins, there is a 1 in 16 chance, or 1 in 8 with the [Heroic Epic](pedia:buildings/heroicEpic), that a [great leader](pedia:concepts/leaders) appears, as long as you have no living military leader and the enemy was not barbarian.

Upgrading keeps a unit's experience. It costs 3 gold per shield of difference in one of your cities, uses up the unit's turn, and the unit gains the new type's extra hit points. Since experience is hard to earn, upgrading your veterans is usually wiser than disbanding them.

leaders.title: Great Leaders
leaders.summary: Great leaders born of victory or discovery can form armies or finish a building at once.
leaders.body:
Great leaders are rare units that appear from victory or discovery.

Military leaders: when an Elite unit wins a battle there is a 1 in 16 chance, 1 in 8 with the [Heroic Epic](pedia:buildings/heroicEpic), that a [Leader](pedia:units/leader) joins your civilization. Battles with barbarians never produce one, and you can have only one living military leader at a time, so put each one to work quickly.

A military leader can:
- form an [army](pedia:concepts/armies) in one of your cities, becoming an empty army that land units can join;
- hurry: in a city, it completes the improvement or wonder being built at once (not Wealth) and is spent.

Scientific leaders: when a scientific civilization is the first in the world to discover an advance, there is a 10% chance that a scientific leader appears in its capital. It can finish an improvement or wonder exactly like a military leader, but it can never lead an army, and it does not count against the one-military-leader limit.

Leaders take the names of their civilization's generals or scholars in order, with numerals once the list runs out.

Leaders cannot fight. An enemy that reaches a leader standing alone destroys it, so keep leaders inside cities or under escort while they travel.

Finishing a great wonder with a leader is one of the strongest moves in the game: carry a new leader to a city that has just started a wonder and claim it before your rivals.

armies.title: Armies
armies.summary: An army bundles up to three land units under a great leader and fights with all of them.
armies.body:
An [Army](pedia:units/army) is a single unit that carries up to three land units, four with [The Pentagon](pedia:buildings/pentagon), and fights with all of them.

To make one, move a military [great leader](pedia:concepts/leaders) into one of your cities and order it to form an army; it becomes an empty army. A city with a [Military Academy](pedia:buildings/militaryAcademy) can also build armies directly. You may field one army for every 4 cities you own, and at least one.

Land units with an attack strength join an army standing on their tile. Members take no orders of their own. The army moves at the speed of its slowest member and has blitz, so it can attack more than once a turn while it has moves left.

In battle an army fights member by member. Each round the member with the highest strength × hit points fights and takes any damage; a member at 0 hit points dies, and the army falls only when all its members are dead. Its total hit points are the sum of its members', which makes a full army very hard to beat. Armies never withdraw and never upgrade.

A victorious army unlocks the Military Academy and the [Heroic Epic](pedia:buildings/heroicEpic) for its civilization.

Armies work best with strong, fast attackers: three knights or tanks in one army can take a fortified city that would cost several separate units. Give a battered army a few quiet turns in one of your cities to heal before sending it on.

naval.title: Ships and Transport
naval.summary: Ships fight at sea, bombard coasts and carry armies across the water.
naval.body:
Ships move on water, pay 1 movement point per tile and can enter your own coastal cities. Not every hull can go everywhere: the [Galley](pedia:units/galley) and similar early ships must stay on coast tiles, and others such as the [Caravel](pedia:units/caravel) may not enter ocean. Seafaring civilizations' ships move one tile farther, and so do everyone's with the [Great Lighthouse](pedia:buildings/greatLighthouse) or [Magellan's Voyage](pedia:buildings/magellansVoyage).

Ships with capacity carry land units. A land unit boards by stepping onto a water tile where your transport has room, which costs one movement point, or with Load while both stand in a port. Carried units move with the ship and land by stepping onto an adjacent land tile. Only amphibious units, such as the [Marine](pedia:units/marine) and the Viking [Berserk](pedia:units/berserk), can attack straight from a ship. Carriers carry aircraft, and missile submarines carry missiles.

Cargo shares the ship's fate: when a ship is sunk at sea, everything aboard is lost. Escort your transports.

Ships fight other ships at sea; against targets on land they bombard ([bombard](pedia:concepts/bombard)). A [Harbor](pedia:buildings/harbor) makes new ships veteran and repairs ships fully, and ships heal only in port. A [Coastal Fortress](pedia:buildings/coastalFortress) gives a city's defenders +50% against naval attacks. Ships in a city that is captured are lost with it.

Water also carries trade: harbour cities connect along the coast, across sea after [Astronomy](pedia:techs/astronomy) and across ocean after [Navigation](pedia:techs/navigation).

air.title: Air Power
air.summary: Aircraft fly one mission a turn from cities or carriers: bombing, scouting, rebasing or intercepting.
air.body:
Aircraft are based in your cities or on carriers and never move tile by tile. Each turn an aircraft flies one mission:
- Bomb: bombard a tile within its operational range, with its bombard strength and rate of fire.
- Precision strike: like bombing, but only buildings are hit; needs [Smart Weapons](pedia:techs/smartWeapons).
- Reconnaissance: fly up to twice the range and reveal the tiles within 2 of the target.
- Rebase: move up to twice the range to another of your cities or a carrier with room.
- Intercept: stand guard until it next acts.

Interception: before a bombing or reconnaissance mission resolves, the strongest enemy aircraft on interception duty with the target in range may rise to meet it, with a 50% chance, or 5% against stealth aircraft. The two fight to the death, the interceptor's attack against the intruder's defence, and if the intruder dies the mission fails.

Air defence: a bomber that gets through then meets the best air defence on the target tile, one round of [Flak](pedia:units/flak) (2), [Mobile SAM](pedia:units/mobileSam) (4) or a warship's guns (1 to 3) against its defence. A hit costs a hit point, and a bomber on its last hit point is shot down. In a city with a [SAM Missile Battery](pedia:buildings/samMissileBattery) that shot is doubled and the defenders get +100% against the bombing; the battery itself does not fire.

Other air operations:
- Airdrop: [Paratroopers](pedia:units/paratrooper) that have not moved jump from one of your cities onto a free land tile within range.
- Airlift: a unit flies from a city with an [Airport](pedia:buildings/airport) to another of your cities; each airport sends one unit a turn.

nukes.title: Nuclear Weapons
nukes.summary: Nuclear weapons destroy everything around their target and leave the land poisoned.

barbarians.title: Barbarians and Tribal Villages
barbarians.summary: Barbarian camps raid the unwary, while tribal villages reward the first explorer to find them.
barbarians.body:
Barbarians are a separate player, always at war with everyone. The game settings decide how active they are: sedentary, roaming (the default), restless or raging.

From turn 10, barbarian camps can appear on empty land outside all borders, at least 6 tiles from any city and 4 from any civilized unit. The chance per turn is 4% for sedentary, 6% for roaming, 9% for restless and 14% for raging barbarians, up to a cap that grows with the map. Each camp keeps a fortified guard and, unless the barbarians are sedentary, sends out a raider every 14, 9 or 5 turns on average.

Barbarians use Warriors until any civilization reaches the second era, then Horsemen. Raiders head for the nearest city or unit within 8 tiles and attack when they like their chances. Barbarians do not keep cities: entering an undefended city they steal up to 10 gold per citizen, kill a citizen and leave. They never destroy a city: a size-1 city keeps its last citizen. From turn 40, barbarian ships may also land up to 3 raiders near a coastal city.

Human players fight barbarians with a bonus that depends on difficulty: +800% at Chieftain, +200% at Regent, +25% at Demigod and nothing above. Entering an empty camp destroys it for 25 gold.

Tribal villages are scattered across the map. The first land unit to enter one may find gold, a map of the area, a free Warrior or an advance. Sometimes the village is empty, and away from your cities it may even release a few barbarians.

capture.title: Capturing Cities and Units
capture.summary: Taking a city brings plunder and buildings, while defenceless units may be captured or destroyed.

warWeariness.title: War Weariness
warWeariness.summary: Under representative governments, long and bloody wars slowly turn your people against you.

diplomacy.title: Diplomacy
diplomacy.summary: Contact, war and peace, treaties, deals, reputation and attitude govern how civilizations deal with each other.
diplomacy.body:
You meet another civilization when a unit, city or border of yours comes into sight of theirs, or when a third civilization introduces you. You start at peace.

War can be declared by either side alone. It ends every treaty and running deal between the two, and the victim does not forget. Peace needs both sides to agree; a peace treaty binds for 20 turns and sends both sides' units home from each other's land. A ceasefire stops a war for 16 turns.

Treaties:
- Right of passage ([Map Making](pedia:techs/mapMaking)): units may stay in each other's land without offence.
- Alliance against a third civilization ([Writing](pedia:techs/writing)): both fight the common enemy.
- Mutual protection pact and trade embargo ([Nationalism](pedia:techs/nationalism)).

Deals can include gold, gold per turn for 20 turns, advances, world maps, contacts, embassies, luxury and strategic resources for 20 turns (even your last copy, which leaves you without it while the deal runs), cities other than the capital, and treaties. At war only a deal containing peace or a ceasefire is possible. A partner who cannot pay a running deal defaults and loses reputation.

Demands: a leader whose city is threatened by your troops in its land may demand that you withdraw them or face war; accepting sends all your units there home at once. A strong leader who dislikes you may now and then demand tribute (gold or an advance) and may go to war if you refuse. A demand left unanswered counts as refused.

Reputation runs from 0 to 100 and falls when you break your word: declaring war while a treaty binds you (up to 40 for a peace or an alliance), cancelling running trade deals by war, or defaulting on a payment. Every civilization that knows you holds the full breach against you, and reputation recovers only a point every ten turns.

Attitude shows how each leader feels about you, from furious through annoyed, cautious and polite to gracious. It reflects remembered events, common enemies, treaties, trade, crowded borders and the leader's temperament; the diplomacy screen lists every reason.

espionage.title: Espionage
espionage.summary: Embassies and spies reveal rivals' secrets, steal their knowledge and stir up their cities.
espionage.body:
Every mission costs its base cost × 3 × (era + 1) gold, so espionage grows dearer as the ages pass. The missions:
- Establish embassy: always succeeds once you have contact and [Writing](pedia:techs/writing) and are not at war. It shows their treasury, government and research and reveals their capital.
- Investigate city (90%): see a city's surroundings and what it is building.
- Steal technology (50%): a random advance they know and you can use.
- Steal world map (70%) and steal plans (60%), which reveals where all their units stand.
- Sabotage production (50%): the city loses its shields.
- Plant spy (75%): needs an embassy and an [Intelligence Agency](pedia:buildings/intelligenceAgency).
- Propaganda: persuade a city other than the capital to defect with its garrison.
- Expose enemy spy (60%): needs an Intelligence Agency.

Investigating a city and stealing technology need an embassy or a planted spy; the other missions need a spy.

Propaganda's chance comes from how the city's people see your culture, from 3% if they are disdainful of you to 30% if they are in awe. Strong culture makes it a cheap way to win cities without a war.

An Intelligence Agency in the target civilization lowers every chance by 20 points. A failed mission still costs the gold, a planted spy that fails is caught and lost, and the victim remembers it (−20 attitude). Stealing, sabotage and propaganda are resented even when they succeed. Embassies can also be traded in deals ([diplomacy](pedia:concepts/diplomacy)).

goldenAges.title: Golden Ages
goldenAges.summary: Once per game a civilization enjoys twenty turns of extra shields and commerce.
goldenAges.body:
Every civilization gets one golden age per game.

It starts with whichever comes first:
- one of your unique units wins a battle for the first time, attacking or defending (a retreating enemy counts as a win);
- the great wonders you hold together carry the characteristics of both your traits. One wonder may cover both: the [Pyramids](pedia:buildings/pyramids) count as a place of worship and as a construction, so they start Egypt's golden age on their own.

The golden age lasts 20 turns. While it lasts, every tile that yields at least one shield yields one more, and every tile that yields at least one commerce yields one more. The bonus comes after the Despotism penalty, so it is never lost to it.

Because a unique unit's first victory is so easy to arrange, timing matters. An ancient unique unit, such as the [Legionary](pedia:units/legionary), can bring a golden age very early while your empire is still small; waiting until you have many cities, roads and mines makes the same twenty turns worth far more. Late unique units such as the [Panzer](pedia:units/panzer) or the [F-15](pedia:units/f15) promise a rich modern golden age, but only if you get that far.

To hold it back, keep your unique units out of fights, remembering that a defensive win counts too. The wonder trigger is harder to plan around: completing the wrong pair of wonders can start the golden age before you are ready. Each civilization's page lists its traits, and each wonder's page its characteristics.

pollution.title: Pollution and Global Warming
pollution.summary: Industry and crowded cities pollute the land, and widespread pollution warms the whole world.
pollution.body:
A city's pollution points come from two sources:
- industry: the pollution of its buildings (Factory 2, Manufacturing Plant 2, Coal Plant 2, Offshore Platform 2, Iron Works 4, and 1 each for a Research Lab, Airport or Commercial Dock) × its shields ÷ 40. A [Recycling Center](pedia:buildings/recyclingCenter) leaves only a third;
- people: once you know [Industrialization](pedia:techs/industrialization), one point per two citizens above size 12. A [Mass Transit System](pedia:buildings/massTransitSystem) removes them.

Each turn a city has a 4% chance per point, at most 90%, to pollute a random unpolluted land tile in its work area. Polluted tiles lose yield until a worker cleans them with [Clear Damage](pedia:workerJobs/clearDamage). The city screen shows the points and where they come from.

Meltdowns: a city with a [Nuclear Plant](pedia:buildings/nuclearPlant) that falls into civil disorder has a 10% chance each turn of a meltdown. Half its people die, at least one survives, the plant is lost and about half the land around is polluted. Keep nuclear cities content.

Global warming: every polluted tile and crater in the world adds a point of warming each turn. When the total passes a threshold (the map's tiles ÷ 50, at least 10, times the number of strikes so far plus one), the climate strikes: one land tile in 200 changes, grassland to plains, plains to desert, forest to plains, jungle to marsh, tundra to plains, and loses its irrigation.

Warming falls on everyone, polluter or not, so cleaning up quickly is in every civilization's interest.

spaceship.title: The Space Race
spaceship.summary: Build and launch a spaceship; the first to reach Alpha Centauri wins.
spaceship.body:
The space race is won by the first civilization whose spaceship arrives at Alpha Centauri.

To begin you need your own [Apollo Program](pedia:buildings/apolloProgram), a small wonder each civilization builds for itself. After that your cities can build the ten spaceship parts, and the ship needs one of each:
- [SS Cockpit](pedia:buildings/ssCockpit), [SS Docking Bay](pedia:buildings/ssDockingBay) and [SS Exterior Casing](pedia:buildings/ssExteriorCasing);
- [SS Engine](pedia:buildings/ssEngine), [SS Thrusters](pedia:buildings/ssThrusters) and [SS Fuel Cells](pedia:buildings/ssFuelCells);
- [SS Life Support System](pedia:buildings/ssLifeSupportSystem), [SS Stasis Chamber](pedia:buildings/ssStasisChamber), [SS Storage/Supply](pedia:buildings/ssStorageSupply) and [SS Planetary Party Lounge](pedia:buildings/ssPlanetaryPartyLounge).

A finished part joins the ship instead of standing in the city, and no city can start a part the ship already has. Spread the work over your best production cities and build the parts side by side; a leader can finish one at once.

When all ten are complete, launch the ship from the victory screen (F8). It leaves from your capital and arrives 12 turns later, and you win at the end of the arrival turn. Computer players launch the moment their ship is ready.

If your capital is captured or destroyed, the ship and every part are lost, whether in flight or still on the ground. A rival who sees a launch has twelve turns to reach your capital, so give it a strong garrison and good walls for the whole race.

If space victory is switched off for the game, spaceship parts cannot be built.

victory.title: Victory and Game Modes
victory.summary: There are six ways to win, and game modes that change what knocks a civilization out.
victory.body:
Victory is checked at the end of every turn, and the first condition met decides the game. Every condition except the histograph can be switched off when starting a game.

- Conquest: every other civilization is gone.
- Domination: 66% of the world's land tiles inside your borders and 66% of its citizens.
- Space race: your spaceship arrives ([spaceship](pedia:concepts/spaceship)).
- Cultural: 100000 culture points and at least twice any rival's, or 20000 in a single city.
- Diplomatic: elected by the [United Nations](pedia:buildings/unitedNations). While someone holds it, an election is held at the end of the turn it is built and every 10 turns after. The candidates are the owner and the most populous other civilization; every civilization votes with its citizens and more than half of all votes wins.
- Histograph: when the last turn (540, AD 2050) ends, the highest score wins.

Game modes change what knocks a civilization out:
- Regicide: each civilization has a king unit; when it dies the civilization is out and its cities surrender to the killer.
- Mass regicide: two kings each; out when both are dead.
- Elimination: a civilization is out as soon as it loses any city, and its other cities surrender to the conqueror.
- Victory points: 10 per wonder, 5 per defeated unit, 5 per first discovery and 100 per conquered city; 50000 points, or the most when time runs out, wins.

Culture flips can also be switched off in the game options.

automation.title: Automation
automation.summary: Governors, templates, the worker pool, unit routines and your own rules take routine work off your hands.
automation.body:
Automation hands routine work to the game without taking control from you. It only gives the orders you could give yourself, and every order carries a reason that appears in the log, the city screen and the turn digest.

Delegation: seven switches choose what automation runs: citizens, builds, workers, research, tax rates, military and diplomacy. A city's own governor or template applies either way.

Governors place a city's citizens by weights for food, shields, commerce, gold, science and luxury, plus a food target. Presets are Balanced, Growth, Production, Gold, Science, Culture, Military Pump and Settler Pump, or set your own weights. Governors can rush builds from a gold budget you set and end disorder with entertainers.

Templates choose builds: an ordered list of buildings, units or unit roles (best defender, attacker, siege unit, ship, worker, settler, explorer) with conditions such as size, food surplus, corruption or being at war. New, coastal and captured cities receive their own templates automatically.

The worker pool: delegated workers share one job board covering every city's needs, ordered by your task priorities, and you can mark regions where some jobs are forbidden ([workers](pedia:concepts/workers)).

Unit routines: explore, auto-work, auto-settle, garrison, patrol, rally, bombard, front, escort and air defence. Your own rules add more: when a trigger fires (a city grew, a unit was built…) and the conditions hold, take an action.

The turn digest lists what needs you, such as threats, disorder, offers, idle cities and units or lost resources, and what automation handled.

difficulty.title: Difficulty Levels
difficulty.summary: Eight levels, from Chieftain to Sid, change your citizens' mood and the computer players' head start.
difficulty.body:
There are eight difficulty levels: Chieftain, Warlord, Regent, Monarch, Emperor, Demigod, Deity and Sid. Regent is the even middle ground.

What changes for everyone:
- Content citizens per city: 4 at Chieftain, 3 at Warlord, 2 at Regent and Monarch, 1 from Emperor up.
- The optimal city number is the world size's value × a percentage, from 100% at Chieftain down to 50% at Sid, so corruption and empire-size unhappiness bite sooner on harder levels.
- Anarchy is capped at 4 turns at Monarch, 3 at Emperor, 2 at Demigod and Deity and 1 at Sid.

What helps you: your units fight barbarians with a bonus of +800% at Chieftain, +400% at Warlord, +200% at Regent, +100% at Monarch, +50% at Emperor and +25% at Demigod.

What helps the computer players:
- extra defenders, attackers, settlers and workers at the start, up to 12 extra defenders and 6 attackers at Sid;
- extra units supported for free, up to 24 plus 8 per city at Sid;
- cheaper research: you always pay Regent's cost factor of 10, while they pay 20 at Chieftain down to 4 at Sid;
- better trades among themselves than with you.

Above Regent the computer players also ask a growing margin when trading with humans, 5% per level, and are a little warier of human ambition. The rules of the game itself never change: harder levels win by head start and efficiency, not by hidden bonuses in battle.
